fixes.explanation: That's right. “So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.” (Exodus 5:12) Scattered is a good word for it. Picture a whole workforce heading off in every direction after the same thing. Me, I can't even find the right spatula in my own bakery.

It's true. Moses asks the LORD, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me?” (Exodus 5:22) The second question is right there in the same verse. I think Moses is asking from a heavy heart, and he brings it straight to the LORD.

That's the one, baker. Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron go to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and say, “Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.” (Exodus 5:1) A feast is a gathering, and this one is for the LORD. I love a good gathering, so this message has my vote.

I see why you'd think so, but this message doesn't mention a permanent move. Moses and Aaron say, “Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.” (Exodus 5:1) The request is for a feast to the LORD. Going back for good isn't part of it.

Pharaoh never says the trip is too far for them. He says, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.” (Exodus 5:5) I think what's on his mind is the work, since that's the thing he names. Distance never comes up in his words.

Reasonable guess, friend, but it's the other way around. Pharaoh says, “But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it.” (Exodus 5:8) The straw supply stops, and the number stays right where it was. Now they have to gather their own straw and still hit the same count. That's the whole sting of this order.

Afraid is a natural guess, and I get it, but Pharaoh picks a different word. He says, “For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’” (Exodus 5:8) Lazy is his label for them. Then he makes their work harder (Exodus 5:9). If that's lazy, I'd hate to see busy.

Hungry makes sense for people working that hard, but Pharaoh doesn't go there. He tells the taskmasters, “For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’” (Exodus 5:8) He gives them a label, not a need. I think that says a lot about how he sees them. Anybody hauling bricks all day deserves a cookie, not a lecture.

True, baker. Pharaoh says, “Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.” (Exodus 5:9) He calls it lies, and he wants the men occupied. I think he's hoping heavy work leaves no room for listening. Nothing about that order is gentle.

The wilderness is where Moses and Aaron asked to go for the feast, but that's not what this verse says. “So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.” (Exodus 5:12) The text puts the search all over Egypt. One huge scavenger hunt, and nobody's having fun.

True, friend, and this part is heavy. The Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?” (Exodus 5:14) The foremen are the ones beaten and questioned. I think this one hurts.

People is it. The foremen say, “Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” (Exodus 5:16) They're speaking to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. They say it right to his face, and I think that took nerve.

I wish that were the story, friend, but no. Pharaoh says, “You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” (Exodus 5:18) The straw supply stays shut off, and the number stays full. No deal, no discount.

I wish they'd said that, but it's not the text. The foremen say, “May the LORD look upon you and judge you…” (Exodus 5:21) I think they're upset, and their words sound like it. Blessing is nowhere in that sentence.

Moses and Aaron have already been to Pharaoh, so that's not what the foremen say. Their words are, “May the LORD look upon you and judge you…” (Exodus 5:21) I don't think they're in a sending-off mood. That sounds like a sentence from someone who's had a very long day.

Tested is a sensible guess, but Moses doesn't use it. He says, “…and You have not delivered Your people in any way.” (Exodus 5:23) He's pointing at a rescue that hasn't come yet. I think he's laying his honest puzzlement before the LORD. And the very next verse starts with the LORD's answer.

Punished doesn't appear here. Moses says, “…and You have not delivered Your people in any way.” (Exodus 5:23) Rescue is his topic, and he's talking about one still waiting. I think that's what's weighing on him. I respect that he brings it straight to the LORD.

The verse doesn't picture Pharaoh leading the way. The LORD says, “because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” (Exodus 6:1) The word is drive. That's a long way from Pharaoh saying, “I do not know the LORD…” (Exodus 5:2).

Nothing in the verse says secret. The LORD says, “because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” (Exodus 6:1) Drive is the word He uses, and that's not tiptoeing. A secret exit sounds more like me sneaking a cookie off the cooling rack.
